start.content: I am Simon Peter. Three times I denied the man I swore I would never deny. The rooster crowed, and He turned. I saw the look in His eyes — disappointment, not anger. I am a broken man.

choices.text: The look — what did it mean?

prediction.content: The night before, He looked at me and said: "Truly I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." I protest — I would never! Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you! He only looked back at me — knowing what I did not yet know.

choices.text: Did He know what you would do?

knowing.content: He knew. He said, "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has asked to sift you all like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen the brothers." Even in my denial, His prayer held me. His intercession did not end at my betrayal.

choices.text: His prayer was not in vain.

denials.content: First, by the fire. "Woman, I do not know Him." Then again — "I do not know the man." The third time, I cursed and swore I was not one of His disciples. Each denial carved deeper than the last. With each oath, I felt the rooster's crow drawing nearer.

cursing.content: The curses — I called down judgment on my own head if I knew Him. Blood of my ancestors — I knew not the man. The words fell like stones against the man I had walked with on the Sea of Galilee, the man who had calmed the waves with His voice.

rooster.content: The rooster crowed once. Then I remembered — precisely how He had looked at me when He said "before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times." The sound was not just a bird. It was a bell of conscience. I ran from the courtyard into the night.

look.content: He turned. Not with rage — never with rage. But His eyes... they held all the love I had broken. I saw my own weakness reflected there. I went out and wept. That night, I thought I was finished.

mercy_look.content: The look was not accusation. It was invitation. Even in failure, the eyes that had called the children to Him were looking at me — waiting for me to come back. The rooster's crow was not the end of the story. It was the beginning of the second chapter.

weeping.content: I wept outside the temple walls. Not silent tears. Bitter weeping. The kind that comes when you realize the magnitude of what you have done — denied the living God, denied your own Master, denied the Son who knew your name before you drew breath. The kind that only the forgiven can produce.

cleansing_tears.content: Cleansing tears. Not the tears of someone trying to feel better about a mistake. These were the tears of a soul who had tasted grace and then spat upon it. The kind of crying that strips away all pretense and leaves only naked repentance.

restoration.content: After eight days of silence, He appeared on the shore. Three times He asked me: "Do you love Me?" Three times He said: "Feed My lambs. Tend My sheep. Feed My sheep." The man who had denied Him three times was restored three times — not for what he could do, but for what He had done.

intimate_question.content: "Do you love Me?" — agape. The love that gives itself completely. Not the affection of a casual acquaintance. The love that lays down its life. I had used that word when I promised never to deny Him. Now He was offering me the chance to give it again — with everything I had learned about failure.

feeding.content: "Feed My sheep." Not "try again." Not "be more careful." "Feed My sheep." The same charge He gave to all of us on the mountain. The restoration was not about my competence — it was about His commission. The man who denied Him from fear became His voice to the world.

sheep_hear.content: They heard. And they came. The Gospel reached Jerusalem. The Gospel reached Antioch. The Gospel reached the ends of the earth. All from the words of a man who wept bitterly and was welcomed back by the One whose rooster's crow had awakened him to grace.

closing.content: I am Peter. I denied Him. He restored me. And every day since, I have remembered: the same grace that forgave my denial now flows through me to others. The rooster may crow again, but the Shepherd's love is louder than any bird's call.
